source.title: Towards a theory of inference-time alignment with unknown rewards
source.authors: Steve Hanneke; Hon-Gao Wang; Mingyue Xu

page_placements.theme: Theory refinements beyond 'must beat' (loss equivalence, bound tightness, limits under concept shift, boosting a weak generator)

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It gives theoretical results about when a weak reference policy can be used to learn a selector with high alignment success, but uses a different inference-time selection setup rather than the original fine-tuning and PGR method.
record.gate_note: The paper does not fine-tune a strong pretrained model on labels produced by a weak model, and reports no PGR or empirical model results. Its own theorems and constructed examples address the theoretical learnability and limitations of weak-reference alignment (V5). Results cited from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper calls inference-time alignment a 'weak-to-strong learning problem', but the construct differs from the claim. The weak reference policy only generates candidate responses. All training labels come from the true target reward r*, not from a weak model. So no student learns from a weaker supervisor's labels, and nothing shows whether a student beats imperfect supervision. This is boosting a weak generator with ground-truth binary labels. Its theorems characterise PAC learnability of best-response selection (finite alignment dimension), which bears on no version, including V5. There are no empirical models and no PGR. The finding belongs under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that in a realizable binary-reward inference-time alignment framework, a reward class is alignment learnable iff its alignment dimension is finite. They present this as an initial theoretical step, with no empirical experiments.
record.recipe_differences: The paper learns a partial pairwise comparator from target-reward acceptance labels and selects among reference-policy samples at inference time; it does not fine-tune a strong model on weak-model labels or measure PGR.
record.method_sensitivity: The stated learnability result depends on the reward class having finite alignment dimension; the theorem's sample and slate requirements depend on d, γ, ϵ, and δ.

fits_no_version.finding: For realizable binary rewards, selecting a good response from k reference-policy samples using ground-truth acceptance labels is PAC learnable iff the alignment dimension is finite. The learner is a pairwise tournament. ERM, learn-and-optimize and pessimism rules each fail on constructed examples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Boosting a weak generator (reference policy with coverage γ) to arbitrarily high selection accuracy, using true-reward labels, is possible exactly for reward classes with finite alignment dimension.

record.problems: The results are theoretical rather than empirical. The main characterization assumes realizable binary rewards and multiple reference-policy samples per prompt in both training and testing. The paper identifies optimal sample-complexity dependencies and single-response training as open questions. It does not directly compare the learned selector's performance with the reference policy's actual performance or calculate PGR.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for cited results or related-work descriptions. The remaining theoretical discussion does not report additional outcomes directly measuring the tested version beyond the theorem statements and constructed examples recorded above.

untested.parts: No strong model fine-tuned on weak-model labels; no PGR.
No auxiliary confidence loss, ensembling or loss variants.
No size, task or representation analysis.
No exploitation, distribution-shift or error-similarity analysis.
Training labels are ground truth, not weak-supervisor labels. No theory is given on when a student trained on a weaker model's labels must beat that supervisor.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' and V5 labels are overturned. The paper borrows the 'weak-to-strong' term for a boosting-style setting where the weak model only generates candidates and labels come from the true reward r*. No weak supervisor's labels are learned from, and the original paper is not cited. Purely theoretical; preprint.

versions.untested_parts: No strong-model fine-tuning on weak-model labels, supervisor comparison, or PGR measurement.
No auxiliary confidence loss, weak-supervisor ensembling, or loss-variant comparison.
No sweep over model size, tasks, or learned representations.
No tests of student exploitation, distribution shift, or error similarity between weak and strong models.

The theory concerns binary realizable reward classes and inference-time selection from reference-policy samples; it does not establish a direct performance comparison with the reference policy in every instance, nor address the original fine-tuning/PGR setup.
No vision or other non-language modality experiments.

rows.subject: pairwise tournament procedure (Theorem 2)
rows.operation_detail: Theorem gives a high-probability alignment guarantee for learning pairwise comparisons and selecting a tournament winner.

conditions.value: m satisfies Equation (7), with stated order Õ((k²/ϵ²)(d+log(1/δ)))

rows.measure: Probability the selected response is accepted by the target reward
rows.baseline: Reference policy generates a good response with probability at least γ for almost every prompt.
rows.note: This is a theoretical guarantee for selection, not an empirical result or a direct comparison against the reference policy's actual success rate.
rows.check: Theorem 2 is a learnability guarantee for selection trained on true-reward acceptance sets. No weak supervisor's labels are involved, so it cannot show a student beating its supervisor (V5). It is the paper's own method guarantee.

source_check.correct: Theorem 2 specifies k≥max{2,⌈(1/γ)log(2/ϵ)⌉} and m≥C(k²/ϵ)[(d∨1)log²((d∨1)k/ϵ)+log(1/δ)]. The stated sufficient order is Õ((k²/ϵ)(d+log(1/δ))).
source_check.problem: The recorded slate threshold doubles the stated coefficient, and the recorded sample-complexity order uses 1/ϵ² instead of 1/ϵ.

rows.subject: arbitrary learning algorithm (Theorem 3)
rows.operation_detail: Lower-bound construction showing non-learnability when the alignment dimension is infinite.

conditions.value: any finite slate size k and training sample size m

rows.measure: Test alignment error and probability of exceeding the error threshold
rows.value: The construction gives test error at least ϵ with probability at least 2/7; hence the class is not alignment learnable.
rows.note: This establishes a boundary on learnability, rather than measuring PGR or strict improvement over the supervisor.
rows.check: Theorem 3 is an impossibility result for infinite alignment dimension in the same ground-truth-label setting, not a condition on student-versus-supervisor performance. The 'partial' state is also not meaningful for a theorem.

rows.subject: ERM followed by test-time reward optimization (Example 1)
rows.operation_detail: ERM learns a reward function from the sample, then test-time selection optimizes according to the learned reward.

conditions.value: Example 1; infinite VC dimension and d_ALN(R)=0

rows.measure: Whether the procedure selects an accepted response on the stated construction
rows.baseline: A test-time strategy that returns y(0) if present and otherwise y(1) is stated to be alignment learnable without training samples.
rows.value: The worst-case ERM predictor selects y(1) at an unseen xi and is always wrong there.
rows.note: Constructed theoretical example; no empirical model is evaluated.
rows.check: Example 1 is a constructed counterexample showing ERM plus test-time optimisation fails. It rules out a candidate algorithm and characterisation, and bears on no weak-to-strong version.

rows.subject: learn-and-optimize strategies (Example 2)
rows.operation_detail: The paper analyzes any strategy that first learns a binary reward function independent of the test instance and then optimizes it on the candidate pool.

conditions.value: xi absent from training data; candidate pool contains two distinct responses
si uniformly sampled from [2p]; πref samples y(si) and y(si+1) equally

rows.measure: Expected binary reward-classification error on the test prompt
rows.value: For any learned binary reward function, the expected error over s is at least 1/2.
rows.note: The stated result concerns the learn-and-optimize principle for this construction.
rows.check: Example 2 is a constructed counterexample to the learn-and-optimize principle under ground-truth labels, not a weak-supervision result.

rows.subject: test-aware pessimism principle (Example 2)
rows.operation_detail: Uses the test candidate pool and pessimistically selects the smallest-indexed response when multiple distinct responses appear.

conditions.value: one unique response, or at least two distinct responses

rows.measure: Whether the selected response is good under the target reward
rows.value: The paper states that this strategy realizes alignment learnability for Example 2; with one unique response it is good under the stated coverage condition, and with multiple distinct responses the smallest-indexed response is guaranteed good.
rows.note: A theoretical construction, not a model experiment.
rows.check: This is a constructed example where test-aware pessimism succeeds. It concerns algorithm design for selection, not a student surpassing a weak supervisor's labels.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.3, opening discussion of Example 2 and test-aware version space, pp. 9–10.

rows.subject: pessimism principle (Example 3)
rows.operation_detail: Applies the test-aware version-space pessimism rule to a candidate pool containing both responses at an unseen prompt.
rows.measure: Whether the pessimistic reward estimate permits selection of a good response
rows.value: The version space contains both reward patterns (1,0) and (0,1); the pointwise-minimum estimate assigns 0 to both responses and cannot return a good response.
rows.note: The paper states that this construction has infinite VC dimension and alignment dimension 1.
rows.check: Example 3 is a constructed counterexample showing pessimism fails. It bears on no version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: The authors describe their framework as weak-to-strong learning, but the reference policy generates candidates rather than supervisory labels; the results concern a different construct.

tranche.reason: The paper characterizes inference-time selection learned from target-reward acceptance labels. It neither tests nor uses students learning from weaker supervisors' labels, including the student-versus-supervisor conditions named by V5.

source_check.notes: These are theoretical selection guarantees and constructed counterexamples, with no empirical model experiments. Several check-pack fields are truncated; their checks cover the visible claims.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Finite alignment dimension, including the Theorem 2 setting and the stated successful Example 2 construction
reader_labels.reason: Theorem 2 guarantees success probability at least 1−ϵ for finite d_ALN with suitable k and m (r1); the paper also gives a learnable construction where test-aware pessimism succeeds (r5).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Infinite alignment dimension or the specified ERM, learn-and-optimize, and pessimism constructions
reader_labels.reason: Infinite alignment dimension precludes learnability (r2); the examples show that ERM/learn-and-optimize or pessimism can fail in particular constructions (r3, r4, r6).
